'''Andrew Eric Gelman''' (born February 11, 1965) is an American [[statistician]] who is Higgins Professor of Statistics and a professor of [[political science]] at [[Columbia University]]. Gelman attended the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] as a [[National Merit Scholar]], and graduated with [[Bachelor of Science]] degrees in mathematics and in physics in 1986. He then received a [[Master of Science]] degree in 1987 and a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] in 1990, both in statistics from [[Harvard University]], under the supervision of [[Donald Rubin]].<ref>{{MathGenealogy|34263}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Gelman |first=Andrew Eric |title=Topics in Image Reconstruction from Emission Tomography|url=http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/phd_thesis.pdf |access-date=2022-10-01|website=[[Harvard University]]|archive-date=2022-06-06 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220606163108/http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/phd_thesis.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Kesselman|first1=Ellie|title=Statistics comes to Swarthmore College |url=https://myindigolives.wordpress.com/2014/09/10/statistics-at-swarthmore-college-young-tufte-visits/ |access-date=19 November 2016 |date=10 September 2014 |quote=...familiar name on that very short list of all Harvard Statistics PhD alumni: Columbia University political science and statistics professor Andrew Gelman in 1990 |archive-date=30 August 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170830102444/https://myindigolives.wordpress.com/2014/09/10/statistics-at-swarthmore-college-young-tufte-visits/|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Career ==
Gelman is the Higgins Professor of Statistics and Professor of Political Science and the Director of the Applied Statistics Center at Columbia University.<ref>{{cite web |title=Andrew Gelman {{!}} ISERP |url=https://iserp.columbia.edu/people/andrew-gelman |website=iserp.columbia.edu |access-date=12 December 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Applied Statistics Center {{!}} ISERP |url=https://iserp.columbia.edu/center/applied-statistics-center |website=iserp.columbia.edu |access-date=12 December 2022}}</ref> He is a major contributor to statistical philosophy and methods especially in [[Bayesian statistics]]<ref>Andrew Gelman, John B. Carlin, Hal S. Stern and Donald B. Rubin. "''Bayesian Data Analysis''" (2nd edition). Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2003. {{ISBN|978-1-58488-388-3}}</ref> and [[Bayesian hierarchical modeling|hierarchical models]].<ref>{{Cite journal|author=Gelman, Andrew|date=2006|title=Multilevel (hierarchical) modeling: What it can and cannot do |journal=Technometrics |volume=48 |issue=3 |url=https://stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/multi2.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060506015550/http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/multi2.pdf|archive-date=6 May 2006|url-status=live|doi=10.1198/004017005000000661|pages=432–435|s2cid=7974250}}</ref>

He is one of the leaders of the development of the statistical programming framework [[Stan (software)|Stan]].

=== Perspective on Statistical Inference and Hypothesis Testing ===
Gelman's approach to statistical inference emphasizes studying variation and the associations between data, rather than searching for [[statistical significance]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Gelman |first1=Andrew |title=Regression and Other Stories |last2=Hill |first2=Jennifer |last3=Vehtari |first3=Aki |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2022 |pages=59}}</ref>

Gelman says his approach to hypothesis testing is "(nearly) the opposite of the conventional view"<ref>{{Cite web |title=What hypothesis testing is all about. (Hint: It's not what you think.) |url=https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2017/05/04/hypothesis-testing-hint-not-think/ |access-date=2022-02-10 |website=statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu |language=en-US |archive-date=2022-02-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220210144817/https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2017/05/04/hypothesis-testing-hint-not-think/ |url-status=live }}</ref> of what is typical for statistical inference. While the standard approach may be seen as having the goal of rejecting a null hypothesis, Gelman argues that you can't learn much from a rejection. On the other hand, a non-rejection tells you something: "[it] tells you that your study is noisy, that you don't have enough information in your study to identify what you care about—even if the study is done perfectly, even if measurements are unbiased and your sample is representative of your population, etc. That can be some useful knowledge, it means you're off the hook trying to explain some pattern that might just be noise." Gelman also works within the context of larger confirmationist and falsificationist paradigms of science.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Confirmationist and falsificationist paradigms of science  |url=https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2014/09/05/confirmationist-falsificationist-paradigms-science/ |access-date=2022-03-31 |website=statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu |language=en-US |archive-date=2022-04-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220404110528/https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2014/09/05/confirmationist-falsificationist-paradigms-science/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

Gelman's approach to statistical inference is a major recurring theme of his work.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Gelman|first1=Andrew|last2=Hill|first2=Jennifer|author2-link=Jennifer Hill|last3=Vehtari|first3=Aki|date=2020-07-23|title=Regression and Other Stories|url=https://www.cambridge.org/highereducation/books/regression-and-other-stories/DD20DD6C9057118581076E54E40C372C|access-date=2022-02-10|publisher=Higher Education from Cambridge University Press|doi=10.1017/9781139161879 |isbn=9781139161879 |s2cid=218968955 |language=en|archive-date=2022-02-10|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220210191717/https://www.cambridge.org/highereducation/books/regression-and-other-stories/DD20DD6C9057118581076E54E40C372C|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Popular press ==
[[File:Andrew Gelman speaking at UW 2017 - A.jpg|thumb|left|Speaking at the [[University of Washington]] in 2017]]
Gelman is notable for his efforts to make political science and statistics more accessible to journalists and to the public. He was one of the primary authors of "The Monkey Cage",<ref>{{cite news |title=Monkey Cage |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/monkey-cage/ |newspaper=The Washington Post |access-date=19 November 2016 |archive-date=19 November 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161119031610/https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/monkey-cage/ |url-status=live }}</ref> blog published by ''[[The Washington Post]]''. The blog is dedicated to providing informed commentary on politics and making political science more accessible.<ref>[https://themonkeycage.org/2007/11/20/why_this_blog/ "Why this blog?"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150315080104/http://themonkeycage.org/2007/11/20/why_this_blog/ |date=2015-03-15 }} ''The Monkey Cage''</ref>

Gelman also keeps his own blog which deals with statistical practices in social science.<ref>Statistical Modeling, Causal Inference, and Social Science: https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/ {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220210083630/https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/ |date=2022-02-10 }}</ref> He frequently writes about Bayesian statistics, displaying data, and interesting trends in social science.<ref>How Do I Make My Graphs?: https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2013/03/15/how-do-i-make-my-graphs/ {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220516192106/https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2013/03/15/how-do-i-make-my-graphs/ |date=2022-05-16 }}</ref><ref>Exponential Increase In The Number of Stat Majors: https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2013/04/21/exponential-increase-in-the-number-of-stat-majors/ {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220405110323/https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2013/04/21/exponential-increase-in-the-number-of-stat-majors/ |date=2022-04-05 }}</ref> According to ''The New York Times'', on the blog "he posts his thoughts on best statistical practices in the sciences, with a frequent emphasis on what he sees as the absurd and unscientific... He is respected enough that his posts are well read; he is cutting enough that many of his critiques are enjoyed with a strong sense of schadenfreude."<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/10/18/magazine/when-the-revolution-came-for-amy-cuddy.html|title=When the Revolution Came for Amy Cuddy|last=Dominus|first=Susan|date=2017-10-18|work=The New York Times|access-date=2017-10-19|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=2020-01-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200103061226/https://www.nytimes.com/2017/10/18/magazine/when-the-revolution-came-for-amy-cuddy.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

Gelman is a prominent critic of poor methodological work and he identifies such work as contributing to the [[replication crisis]].<ref name=":0" />

== Honors ==
He has received the Outstanding Statistical Application award from the [[American Statistical Association]] three times, in 1998, 2000, and 2008.<ref>{{cite web |title=Outstanding Statistical Application Award |publisher=American Statistical Association |url=http://www.amstat.org/awards/outstandingstatisticalapplicationaward.cfm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160408225512/https://www.amstat.org/awards/outstandingstatisticalapplicationaward.cfm|archive-date=8 April 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Pennington |first1=Rosemary |title=Big, If True - Episode 234 |url=https://statsandstories.net/methods/big-if-true |website=Stats + Stories |publisher=Miami University |access-date=12 December 2022 |location=Miami, Ohio |date=2 June 2022}}</ref> He is an elected fellow of the [[American Statistical Association]]<ref>{{cite web |title=ASA Fellows |url=https://ww2.amstat.org/fellows/ |website=American Statistical Association |access-date=12 December 2022 |date=2 May 2022 |quote=Elected Fellow in 1998}}</ref> and the [[Institute of Mathematical Statistics]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Honored IMS Fellows |url=https://imstat.org/honored-ims-fellows/ |website=Institute of Mathematical Statistics |access-date=12 December 2022 |language=en}}</ref> He was elected fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences|American Academy of Arts and Sciences (AAAS)]] in 2020<ref>{{Cite journal|title=AAAS Fellows Elected|url=https://www.ams.org/journals/notices/202007/rnoti-p1051.pdf|journal=Notices of the American Mathematical Society|volume=67|access-date=2020-09-27|archive-date=2020-08-22|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200822201143/https://www.ams.org/journals/notices/202007/rnoti-p1051.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=New Members |url=https://www.amacad.org/new-members-2020 |website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences |access-date=12 December 2022 |language=en |date=2020}}</ref> and the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 2026.<ref>{{Cite web|title=National Academy of Sciences Elects Members and International Members|url=https://www.nasonline.org/news/2026-nas-election/ |website=National Academy of Sciences |access-date=21 June 2026 |language=en|date=2026}}</ref>

and has three children.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.life-after-baby.com/home/the-way-science-worksor-doesnt|title=The way science works…or doesn't|website=Life After |url=http://rationallyspeakingpodcast.org/show/rs-149-susan-gelman-on-how-essentialism-shapes-our-thinking.html |access-date=2018-05-12 |series=Rationally Speaking: Official Podcast of New York City |transcript-url=http://static1.1.sqspcdn.com/static/f/468275/26732425/1450061194013/rs149transcript.pdf
